title: Bruriah and the Wicked Neighbors
summary: Rowdy neighbors keep bothering Rabbi Meir, and he asks God to make them disappear. His wise wife Bruriah shows him that the verse says "let sins cease" and not "sinners", so he prays for the neighbors to change instead. A story about a different way of looking at the people who bother us.
pages: In a little house lived Rabbi Meir and his wife Bruriah. Rabbi Meir was a great sage, and Bruriah was a great sage too. She knew Torah so well that even the sages came to hear her opinion. In the evenings they would sit together, learning and happily debating.

But some wild, annoying people also lived in the neighborhood. They shouted at night, made noise and bothered Rabbi Meir and the neighbors all the time. Nobody could sleep in peace, and every morning Rabbi Meir got up tired and angry.

One day Rabbi Meir couldn't take it anymore. "Enough!" he said. "I will pray that these bad people disappear and are gone for good!" He stood in the corner of the room, closed his eyes and began to pray that God would punish them.

Bruriah heard him and asked gently, "Wait, Meir. Why are you praying like that? Because of the verse 'Let sins cease from the earth'?"
"Yes," answered Rabbi Meir. "It's written in Psalms that they will come to an end."
"But look carefully," Bruriah smiled. "It says 'sins', not 'sinners'!"

What's the difference? "Sinners" are the people who do bad things. "Sins" are the bad deeds themselves. "Let sins cease, not sinners" means: we don't want the people to disappear. We want the bad deeds to disappear, and the people to stay and change.

"And look at the end of the verse," Bruriah went on. "It says 'and the wicked will be no more.' If the sins come to an end, and the neighbors do teshuvah and become good, then of course there won't be any more wicked people! So ask God to have mercy on them, so they will do teshuvah and change their ways."

Rabbi Meir thought for a long moment. His anger slowly melted, like ice in the sun. "You're right," he said. He went back to the corner of the room, and now he prayed in a completely different way: "God, help our neighbors to be good. Give them a new heart."

And what happened? Little by little the neighbors changed. They stopped shouting at night and started saying "Good morning" in the morning. One of them even helped Rabbi Meir carry a heavy sack. The neighborhood became quiet and pleasant, and at last everyone slept in peace.

And you? Sometimes a child at preschool bothers us, grabs or pushes, and we get angry and want them to just disappear. But maybe, like Bruriah, we can think differently: I don't like what he's doing, but he can change. And sometimes a kind word helps more than a big anger.
